robocurve.description: Robocurve builds open-source tools and independent benchmarks to measure how well robots can do real-world jobs. Instead of relying on unverified demo videos from frontier labs, we score their models on reproducible benchmarks that anyone can trust. Today there are no well-run, standardized robotics benchmarks. Labs evaluate in-house, and no independent group has stepped in to run continuous benchmarking as a service. The result is that no one actually knows how good anyone else is, or where the real frontier sits. Good benchmarks require operating and maintaining physical hardware and real-world setups. Simulation only goes so far, since models that look strong in sim can show large performance gaps once deployed in the real world. Building real-world benchmarks means coordinating job-domain experts, evals engineering, and hands-on robotics all at once. Frontier labs are targeting general-purpose robotics by 2028, yet the field of robotics evals barely exists. Whoever builds the trusted measure of robot capability becomes the reference everyone relies on. We combine backgrounds in AI evals and robotics to build and grow this field as fast as possible. We already shipped v1 of our open-source framework, Inspect Robots, and ran our first pilot scoring a frontier model on a real robot.

brief.summary: Salem Robotics sells autonomy software that lets existing mobile robots (Boston Dynamics Spot is one, a co-founder says) run surveys and inspections in hazardous facilities. It started with radiological surveys at nuclear sites and says it is also working on oil, gas and hazardous chemical facilities. The Form D gives an Austin, Texas address.
brief.thesis: Nuclear sites must run routine radiation surveys and largely do them by hand. Salem sells software for robots sites may already own, touching robotics and energy without building hardware. Both founders co-authored a February 2024 paper on robot radiation surveys.
brief.stage: A Form D filed on 8 September 2026 reports $1,819,500 sold of a $5,100,000 SAFE offering to 5 unnamed investors, first sale 13 May 2026. Y Combinator lists the company in its Summer 2026 batch. Non Sibi Ventures is the only other investor confirmed by its own pages (a $25,000 Rice prize investment in April 2026, and it says it backed the company beyond that, no amount given).

questions: Which facilities have signed a paid validation, at what price, and has any converted into an ongoing deployment? The Launch HN post names no customer.
Who are the 5 SAFE investors and what are the caps? How much did Non Sibi invest beyond the $25,000 Rice prize, and is Goose Capital an investor?
Incorporated in 2024 per the Form D, first SAFE sale 13 May 2026. What happened in between, and do UT Austin or Los Alamos hold any rights?

The launch post claims theoretical safety guarantees. What exactly is guaranteed, and has any site radiation protection program or regulator accepted robot-generated survey records as compliance records?
risks: No source shows a signed customer, a paid validation or a deployment. The company's 4 August 2026 launch post speaks of "active contract-scoping conversations" in nuclear and oil and gas.
The product is a software layer on other companies' robots. A robot maker could move into this layer. The founders' Launch HN post asks where the line should sit.
Public records do not line up. Y Combinator says founded 2026 in San Francisco with a team of 2. The Form D says incorporated 2024 with an Austin address.
unverified: The company site shows a Goose Capital logo. No Goose Capital page found confirms an investment, and Rice's 2026 results list its prizes going to other companies.
Non Sibi Ventures says both founders hold top-secret clearances, not confirmed by any primary source.
The launch post says the manipulation framework rests on founder research published in IEEE journals and conferences. Those papers were not located.

review.note: Three-person team (CEO Kamel Greene, CTO Christopher Taylor, one engineer) per USAspending shows only two awards ever, both June 2026 Phase I-size SBIRs; no equity funding found. The entity is older than it looks: FibrX LLC already existed in Dec 2022.

brief.summary: FibrX builds a structural health and corrosion monitoring system that pairs fiber optic sensors with cloud software (a platform-as-a-service, per its site). The sensing method comes from Naval Surface Warfare Center, Port Hueneme Division, and JumpStart says the company operates under a partially exclusive U.S. Navy license. Federal awards list Henderson, Nevada.
brief.thesis: FibrX is trying to turn a Navy-patented method for detecting corrosion under coatings into a monitoring product for defense, aerospace and energy. It holds two small Defense Department R&D awards. The case rests on whether three people can field hardware.
brief.stage: USAspending shows two federal awards to FibrX Inc, both signed in June 2026: an Air Force purchase order for $105,392 (ended 24 September 2026) and a NAVSEA contract labelled SBIR Phase I with $136,573 obligated and $234,840 including options (to 21 June 2027). Chloe Capital announced an investment on 17 February 2026, no amount stated. EDGAR has no filer named FibrX Inc, so no Form D is on record.

questions: Is the Navy patent license signed and in force, does it cover US 11,474,046 B2, and what are the field of use, royalty and milestone terms?
Has a sensor system been installed on a real asset, and what data shows the fiber detects corrosion rather than only strain and temperature?
What is FibrX building under NAVSEA topic N254-P02, an open topic for modular mine warfare components, and how does that work relate to the corrosion monitoring product?
How much equity money has been raised in total and on what terms (IAI CATALYST, Techstars, Chloe Capital, others)?
risks: No customer, pilot or installed system is named on the company's site. Four years after its 2022 startup studio cohort, federal obligations on record total $241,965 across two awards.
The core method is a Navy patent (US 11,474,046 B2), not the company's own. The signed agreement and its terms are not public.
The work is spread wide for three people: hypersonic and space systems (Air Force), naval mine components (NAVSEA topic), and bridges, oil and gas and offshore wind (site marketing).
unverified: A signed Navy patent license rests on the company's site and the JumpStart article, not independently confirmed.
What FibrX received from IAI, Techstars or Chloe Capital is not stated in any source. No amount could be confirmed.
The date and state of incorporation of FibrX Inc, and how it relates to the FibrX LLC in the Navy's 2022 story, are unconfirmed.

hundred.description: Hundred is an automated inspection system for consumer electronics parts. We help factories cut waste and prevent line-down issues by catching sub-millimeter cosmetic defects before parts reach the assembly line. Designs change so fast that traditional vision models can't keep up, meaning factories still rely on manual inspection, literally people checking parts under microscopes to sort out bad parts. Human inspectors miss ~15% of defects which can turn a finished device into scrap. Defects cost U.S. discrete manufacturers $45 billion a year, and Erica saw this problem firsthand designing hardware at Meta, Google, and Magic Leap. She met Imani at Columbia's admitted-students day in 2017, and later met Iris through mutual friends in the Bay Area. Imani spent the last five years at Twitch building software that handles billions of requests a day, and Iris worked in Quant at Citadel before pivoting to research machine learning methods on 3D meshes and other structured data at Imperial College London. Now the team is building Hundred because manual inspection shouldn't exist in 2026.

facts.bio: Erica is co-founder and CEO of Hundred (YC F26). Previously spent 5.5+ years at Meta, Google, and Magic Leap designing hardware for consumer electronics, and resolving issues on the ground with vendors in China and Mexico. Columbia University, BS Mechanical Engineering.

nori.description: We manufacture Nori: A sub-$2000 bimanual mobile manipulator that can clean rooms, restock shelves, and fold clothes. Nori can handle basic tasks out of the box, and its software lets anyone teach Nori to automate work specific to their home or business. Nori aims to solve the robotics data bottleneck. By deploying affordable robots to customers around the world, we can gather the diverse data required to train the next generation of generalist robotic policies. Every user of Nori makes Nori smarter. Since launching 6 weeks ago we have already deployed our first robot and have over $440k+ in sales. We can bring general-purpose robotics to homes and businesses that could never afford it before. There are 132.7 million households and 8.4 million employer business locations in the U.S. At $1,688 per robot, selling just one Nori to 0.5% of them represents a $1.2B market opportunity in the U.S. alone.

facts.bio: Antonio is the founder of Nori Robotics. He also holds a national patent for a computer-vision system, and previously co-founded Truely, which grew to 2,000+ users and 1.5M+ impressions.
